briefings.contentText:
Prioritize patching · Last reviewed Nov 19, 2026

PHP published 17 security advisories on November 19, 2026, including seven critical flaws such as phpAfterShell; several can lead to code execution in specific configurations.

Updates

- Nov 19, 2026: PHP released 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 and 8.6.0 (https://www.php.net/ChangeLog-8.php) with fixes for 17 security advisories, and depthfirst published its phpAfterShell research (https://depthfirst.com/research/phpaftershell).

Details

On November 19, 2026, PHP released 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 and 8.6.0 with fixes for 17 security advisories: seven rated critical (CVSS v4.0 9.2), four high and six medium. This briefing covers the seven critical flaws. In its advance notice, PHP said the critical issues require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups.

phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714) is in PHP's default file-based session handler. If a session write is interrupted, the file can keep the start of the new session and the end of the old one. The next session_start() can then deserialize objects an attacker placed there. Session upload progress is one way for a remote client to shape the stored data, and applications that store large user-controlled strings in sessions are another. PHP's advisory says code execution also needs an interruption at a useful point and a suitable deserialization gadget chain in the application.

depthfirst says it discovered and reported phpAfterShell; the CVE record credits Leo Lin and Asahi as reporters. depthfirst reports that it reached code execution without an application gadget class by chaining a second, undisclosed memory corruption bug in a PHP-native class. The sources reviewed do not establish whether that second bug is fixed in these releases.

CVE-2026-129289 lets an unauthenticated attacker smuggle a second FastCGI request into PHP-FPM and run PHP code as the worker. PHP says this needs a front end that reuses backend connections, such as nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on or HAProxy, and an application path that opens php://input without reading it to the end. The demonstrated attack also needs the path of an existing PHP script. Front ends that close the FastCGI connection after each request are not affected by it. LSAPI shares the cleanup bug, but PHP does not establish code execution there.

CVE-2026-115560, the session serializer mismatch covered in the php2shell briefing, is now fixed, and the fix turns session upload progress off by default. PHP's November 19 advisory widens its scope: no runtime serializer change is needed when separate applications, pools or command-line jobs with different serializers share a session store. CVE-2026-129481 is a use-after-free in PHP 8.3 and later that PHP describes as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-109619; PHP has not demonstrated code execution through it.

CVE-2026-129496 is a use-after-free in non-thread-safe builds. An unauthenticated attacker can crash a fresh worker, and possibly run code, when a startup diagnostic has been written to a PHP error log file. PHP's advisory says code execution was demonstrated locally in PHP-FPM and Apache mod_php with known memory addresses.

CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 are use-after-free bugs in fatal error backtraces, which PHP 8.5 enables by default. Both affect PHP 8.5, and PHP says CVE-2026-129474 also affects later versions. For CVE-2026-129474, PHP notes that the zend.exception_ignore_args=1 setting in php.ini-production blocks the demonstrated attack path. CVE-2026-129182 also needs specific path-level settings and an Apache per-directory configuration or front end that produces an early diagnostic. PHP has not demonstrated code execution through it.

On November 19, 2026, none of the 17 vulnerabilities was in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and no source reviewed reports exploitation in the wild. CISA does list CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 from the October php2shell release. Two of today's critical fixes, for CVE-2026-129481 and CVE-2026-129182, close gaps left by the fix for CVE-2026-109619.

Risk

No source reviewed on November 19, 2026 reports exploitation in the wild. PHP says phpAfterShell affects its default session handler; CVE-2026-129289 allows unauthenticated code execution with FastCGI connection reuse.

Affected deployments

PHP 8.2 before 8.2.36, 8.3 before 8.3.37, 8.4 before 8.4.28, 8.5 before 8.5.13. PHP 8.6.0 contains all 17 fixes; depthfirst and PHP confirm that 8.6.0 release candidates were affected by phpAfterShell and CVE-2026-129474. Whether a deployment is exposed depends on the conditions of each flaw, described in the details.

PHP 8.1 and earlier are end of life. depthfirst says the official 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 end-of-life mitigation branches are not affected by phpAfterShell. PHP's advisories say CVE-2026-129289 was introduced in PHP 5.6.0 and that releases older than 8.2 may also be affected by CVE-2026-115560.

Distribution packages can backport fixes without changing the PHP version number, so check the full package version against the distribution's advisory.

Recommended actions

Upgrade PHP to 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 or 8.6.0 and restart workers. Until then, disable session upload progress and FastCGI connection reuse to remove some attack paths.

1. Find every PHP runtime serving web requests, including container images and managed hosting. For each, record the PHP version, thread safety and server API (FPM, mod_php, CGI or LSAPI), session.save_handler, session.upload_progress.enabled, and whether the front end reuses FastCGI connections. For distribution packages, check the full package version against the distribution's advisory.
   - PHP security advisories: https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories
   - PHP 8 ChangeLog: https://www.php.net/ChangeLog-8.php
2. Upgrade to PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28 or 8.5.13, or move 8.6.0 release candidates to 8.6.0. Rebuild container images and restart the PHP-FPM master or Apache so every worker loads the new binary, then verify the version serving web requests. Move PHP 8.1 and earlier to a supported branch.
   - PHP 8.2.36 release: https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-11-19-1
   - PHP 8.3.37 release: https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-11-19-2
   - PHP 8.4.28 release: https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-11-19-3
   - PHP 8.5.13 release: https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-11-19-4
   - PHP 8 ChangeLog, including 8.6.0: https://www.php.net/ChangeLog-8.php
3. After upgrading, check whether any php.ini, FPM pool or virtual host still sets session.upload_progress.enabled=1, because an explicit setting overrides the new default. If you need the feature, make every reader and writer of the same session store use the same session.serialize_handler.
   - GHSA-658j-r8rw-q6mx: session serializer mismatch (CVE-2026-115560): https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-658j-r8rw-q6mx
4. Until you can upgrade, apply PHP's interim mitigations in the configuration your web workers use, not only the CLI. Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 (CVE-2026-126714, CVE-2026-115560) and limit untrusted data stored in sessions (CVE-2026-126714). Turn off FastCGI connection reuse (CVE-2026-129289). On PHP 8.5 and 8.6.0 release candidates, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and make sure request-specific configuration cannot re-enable it (CVE-2026-129182, CVE-2026-129474). These steps reduce exposure; they do not fix the flaws.
   - GHSA-fm2m-fjf5-v3cp: partially overwritten session files (phpAfterShell) (CVE-2026-126714): https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-fm2m-fjf5-v3cp
   - GHSA-658j-r8rw-q6mx: session serializer mismatch (CVE-2026-115560): https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-658j-r8rw-q6mx
   - GHSA-qc49-hpvq-g2w6: PHP-FPM request smuggling (CVE-2026-129289): https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-qc49-hpvq-g2w6
   - GHSA-2fjv-p558-g82m: use-after-free in fatal error backtrace (CVE-2026-129182): https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-2fjv-p558-g82m
   - GHSA-8mjj-2r7p-4hg2: use-after-free in magic method backtraces (CVE-2026-129474): https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-8mjj-2r7p-4hg2
5. Also until you can upgrade, fix configuration errors and deprecated settings that produce PHP startup warnings, or send PHP errors to syslog instead of a file, then restart PHP (CVE-2026-129496). On PHP-FPM, pm.max_requests=1 blocks the demonstrated CVE-2026-129481 sequence at a performance cost. Keep PHP-FPM listeners off untrusted networks.
   - GHSA-gr4f-wgx5-jpfv: timezone cache use-after-free (CVE-2026-129496): https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-gr4f-wgx5-jpfv
   - GHSA-g3vh-838c-65v7: use-after-free after interrupted session shutdown (CVE-2026-129481): https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-g3vh-838c-65v7
   - GHSA-qc49-hpvq-g2w6: PHP-FPM request smuggling (CVE-2026-129289): https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-qc49-hpvq-g2w6

Use this prompt with an agent that can inspect your infrastructure.

Assess whether the PHP deployments I am authorized to inspect are affected by the critical vulnerabilities PHP fixed on November 19, 2026: CVE-2026-126714 (phpAfterShell), CVE-2026-129289, CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-129496, CVE-2026-129481, CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182. Use the PHP security advisories at github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories and the PHP 8 ChangeLog as authoritative sources. For each host, container image or hosting account, collect: the PHP version (including 8.6.0 release candidates), thread safety and server API serving web requests (not only the CLI), the distribution package version if PHP comes from a distribution, the effective values of session.save_handler, session.upload_progress.enabled, session.serialize_handler, error_log, fatal_error_backtraces and zend.exception_ignore_args and pm.max_requests (including FPM pool and virtual host overrides), and whether the web server reuses FastCGI or LSAPI backend connections (for example nginx fastcgi_keep_conn, Apache mod_proxy_fcgi enablereuse or HAProxy). Report each deployment as affected, fixed or unknown for each CVE, with the evidence, and list anything you could not access. Work read-only: do not change configuration, restart services or send exploit traffic.

Find more information and resources at https://radar.cloudflare.com/zero-wire/php-november-2026-security-release-phpaftershell

Cloudflare coverage

Product coverage

The Cloudflare Free and Managed Rulesets each include a PHP Remote Code Execution Attack rule for phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714), enabled by default with Block as the default action. The Cloudflare Managed Ruleset also includes three rules with Log as the default action: one for CVE-2026-129289 in PHP-FPM, and two for the PHP SOAP flaws CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506, which PHP fixed in the same releases. The rules are a compensating control, not a fix for the vulnerable PHP runtime.

- PHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-126714) #6: Default action: Block · Free plans, Paid plans

briefings.contentText:
Prioritize patching · Last reviewed Nov 19, 2026

A one-byte heap overflow when Ruby changes the case of strings in some single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 and Windows-1252, may let an attacker run code.

Updates

- Nov 19, 2026: Discourse moved its Docker base image to Ruby 4.0.10 (https://github.com/discourse/discourse_docker/commit/400b616aed685afb038c86631228e0a6b5ccd302); Docker installs fix the flaw by rebuilding.
- Nov 19, 2026: Ruby published GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 (https://github.com/ruby/ruby/security/advisories/GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5) and released fixes in Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13 and 4.0.10 (https://www.ruby-lang.org/en/news/2026/11/18/multiple-vulnerabilities-in-regexp-and-string/).

Details

When Ruby upcases the German sharp s (ß) in some single-byte encodings, it writes two bytes, SS, but checks for room for only one. The Ruby fix commit changes 14 ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings, including ISO-8859-1 and Windows-1252. Veria Labs reports that upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp? reach the bug. It says a string with 21 sharp s characters overflows the output buffer by one byte. UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected, according to Veria Labs.

Ruby rates the flaw critical and published it as GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 on November 19, 2026 (UTC). MITRE assigned it CVE-2026-132825 on November 19, 2026. Ruby credits Stephan Lipp (Ada Logics) and Anthropic for reporting it.

Veria Labs reports that Rails and classic-style Sinatra reach the bug in their default configuration, and that other frameworks and plain Rack are not exposed by default. Application code that changes the case of strings received in a legacy encoding may also be affected. As of November 19, 2026, Veria Labs says it will publish a proof of concept in a week. No source reviewed on November 19, 2026 reports exploitation in the wild. Neither Ruby nor Veria Labs lists a workaround or mitigation other than upgrading Ruby.

The same Ruby releases fix six other memory safety flaws in the regular expression engine and string case conversion, several of which Ruby also says may allow code execution.

Risk

The Ruby team is aware of proofs of concept achieving code execution in some scenarios. Veria Labs reports that default Rails and classic Sinatra apps reach the overflow without authentication.

Affected deployments

Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. Veria Labs reports the bug has been present since Ruby 2.4.0. Ruby says that Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive the fix.

As of November 19, 2026 at 08:30 UTC, Veria Labs lists these self-hosted products as bundling an affected Ruby in their latest release: GitLab 19.6.0 (Ruby 3.3.13), GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5 (4.0.9), Mastodon 4.7.5 (4.0.9), OpenProject 17.9.7 (4.0.9), Discourse 2026.10.1 and Chatwoot 4.20.0 (3.4.4). Veria Labs gives Ruby 3.4.7 for Discourse, but the Discourse Docker image used Ruby 4.0.9 before Discourse moved it to the fixed 4.0.10 on November 19, 2026. For products installed from source, the Ruby version is the one the operator installed.

Recommended actions

Upgrade Ruby to 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10 and restart Ruby processes. For self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, install the vendor's update; several had none on November 19, 2026.

1. Find every Ruby runtime you run, including container images and self-hosted software that bundles Ruby, and record the version of each running process. For distribution packages, check the full package version against the distribution's advisory, since a backported fix may keep the old version number.
   - Ruby security advisory: https://www.ruby-lang.org/en/news/2026/11/18/multiple-vulnerabilities-in-regexp-and-string/
2. Upgrade Ruby to 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10. Move applications on Ruby 3.2 or earlier to a supported series, because those releases will not be fixed.

briefings.title: WordPress 7.1.5: Template Part flaw can turn an administrator's click into code execution
briefings.summary: Update affected systems. WordPress released 7.1.5 and fixed releases for every branch back to 4.7. Confirm every site runs WordPress 7.1.5 or the fixed release for its branch, such as 7.0.9 or 6.9.12, and update sites where automatic background updates are off.
briefings.contentText:
Update affected systems · Last reviewed Nov 19, 2026

WordPress 7.1.5 fixes 20 security issues. The most serious can give an attacker an Administrator account, and then code execution, when an Administrator opens a crafted editor link.

Updates

- Nov 18, 2026: WordPress released 7.1.5 (https://wordpress.org/news/2026/11/wordpress-7-1-5-release/) and fixed releases for every branch back to 4.7.

Details

On November 18, 2026, WordPress released 7.1.5 with fixes for 20 security issues, and backported them to every branch back to 4.7. WordPress published 19 GitHub security advisories for them: five rated high, five medium and nine low. The twentieth is a hardening change that removes the Imgur embed variation from the block editor. No CVE IDs had been assigned when this briefing was reviewed.

The most serious issue (GHSA-pmp8-6cv8-q323) is in the Template Part block. Its theme and slug attributes could make an Administrator's editor send requests to another URL on the same site. An unauthenticated attacker can send an Administrator a crafted editor link or redirect them to one, and a user with the Author role or above can set the attributes in a post. When the Administrator opens it, the request can create an Administrator account for the attacker, who can then run code by uploading a plugin. WordPress rates it high and fixed it in all branches back to 5.9.

Three other issues need no account. Visitors could post a comment whose shortcode attribute decoded into HTML after sanitization, which allowed stored cross-site scripting where a Comments or Latest Comments block is placed in post content (GHSA-cr2m-2j4r-3v3x). A single XML-RPC request could batch many pingbacks through system.multicall, each pausing for a second and making an outbound HTTP request, which ties up a PHP worker (GHSA-56j2-5mp6-wr3x). The REST API search endpoint could return terms from private taxonomies, such as navigation menus (GHSA-rcr3-43fx-wqfv).

The release also fixes two SQL injection flaws. One in WP_Meta_Query is reachable only through a plugin or theme that passes untrusted nested meta_query input (GHSA-xc9c-4hg4-h4jg). The other needs the manage_options capability and lets a site Administrator on multisite read the shared database, including network user tables (GHSA-mcv9-c2pg-6m4v). A separate multisite flaw lets a site Administrator take over a Super Admin account on sites with a classic theme and widgets enabled (GHSA-mwj7-xhp9-7773). The remaining fixes cover cross-site scripting, information disclosure and authorization issues that need a signed-in user or a victim's action.

Two of the 19 advisories credit Anthropic as reporter. On November 19, 2026, no source reviewed reported exploitation of these issues, and CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, version 2026.11.18, had no entry for them.

Risk

No source reviewed on November 19, 2026 reports exploitation in the wild. The flaw needs no attacker account, but an Administrator must open the attacker's link while signed in.

Affected deployments

WordPress 7.1 before 7.1.5, 7.0 before 7.0.9, 6.9 before 6.9.12, and older branches back to 4.7 before their November 18, 2026 releases. WordPress says 7.0 back to 6.5 are affected by all 20 issues and older branches by fewer; the Template Part flaw affects 5.9 and later.

WordPress 4.6 and earlier no longer receive security updates. WordPress says only the most recent version is actively supported.

Recommended actions

Confirm every site runs WordPress 7.1.5 or the fixed release for its branch, such as 7.0.9 or 6.9.12, and update sites where automatic background updates are off.

1. List every WordPress site you run, including staging copies and managed hosting accounts, and record its version from Dashboard > Updates. Note which sites have automatic background updates turned off.
   - WordPress 7.1.5 release: https://wordpress.org/news/2026/11/wordpress-7-1-5-release/
2. Update each site to WordPress 7.1.5. If a site must stay on an older branch, install the fixed release for that branch, such as 7.0.9 or 6.9.12; HelpHub lists the fixed release for every branch back to 4.7. Sites with automatic background updates receive the fix without action, but check that the update completed.
   - WordPress 7.1.5 HelpHub: https://wordpress.org/documentation/wordpress-version/version-7-1-5/
   - WordPress releases: https://wordpress.org/download/releases/
3. Move sites on WordPress 4.6 or earlier to a supported branch, because they will not receive these fixes.
   - WordPress 7.1.5 HelpHub: https://wordpress.org/documentation/wordpress-version/version-7-1-5/
4. Until a site is updated, ask Administrators not to open editor links they did not expect. After updating, review the site's Administrator accounts and installed plugins for any you did not add.
   - GHSA-pmp8-6cv8-q323: Template Part block privilege escalation: https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/security/advisories/GHSA-pmp8-6cv8-q323

Use this prompt with an agent that can inspect your infrastructure.

Assess whether the WordPress sites I am authorized to inspect are affected by the 20 security issues fixed in WordPress 7.1.5 on November 18, 2026, in particular the Template Part block privilege escalation GHSA-pmp8-6cv8-q323. Use the WordPress 7.1.5 release post, the version 7.1.5 HelpHub page and the advisories at github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/security/advisories as authoritative sources. For each site, collect: the WordPress version, the fixed release for its branch, whether automatic background updates for minor releases are enabled and whether the latest update completed, whether it is multisite, and whether it runs on WordPress 4.6 or earlier. Report each site as affected, fixed or unknown, with the evidence. Also list Administrator accounts and plugins added since November 1, 2026, so I can check them. List anything you could not access. Work read-only: do not update, change settings, create accounts or send exploit traffic.

Find more information and resources at https://radar.cloudflare.com/zero-wire/wordpress-7-1-5-template-part-privilege-escalation

briefings.contentText:
Prioritize patching · Last reviewed Nov 18, 2026

Five memory corruption flaws in nginx, together called nginx2root, can let an unauthenticated attacker crash a worker process or run code on the server, each in a different configuration.

Updates

- Nov 18, 2026: F5 (https://my.f5.com/manage/s/article/K000164058) and nginx.org disclosed ten nginx vulnerabilities fixed in nginx 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 (https://nginx.org/en/security_advisories.html), including the five Xint calls nginx2root, and Xint published technical details (https://xint.io/blog/nginx2root-remote-code-execution).

Details

On November 18, 2026, F5 and nginx.org disclosed ten nginx vulnerabilities. Xint, which reported five of them, published technical details on those five under the name nginx2root. Each is an independent path to memory corruption in a worker process, in a different configuration. F5 rates each one High (CVSS 3.1 score 8.1) and Critical (CVSS 4.0 score 9.2), and says code execution requires ASLR to be disabled or bypassed. Xint describes leaking memory addresses to bypass it.

CVE-2026-123007 is an overflow in HTTP/2 flow control that leads to out-of-bounds heap reads and writes. It affects any server with HTTP/2 enabled, from nginx 1.9.5. Xint demonstrated command execution against a public HTTPS endpoint on AWS, GCP and Azure, and notes that the HTTP/2 control frames the attack uses are not logged as requests.

CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-121810 are use-after-free flaws in HTTP/2 (from 1.19.7) and HTTP/3 (from 1.25.0) when nginx proxies requests to a backend and a worker runs low on worker_connections. F5 says exploiting the HTTP/3 flaw also depends on conditions beyond the attacker's control. CVE-2026-123634 is a use-after-free in the resolver when proxy_pass uses variables and an SSI or mirror subrequest resolves the same name. CVE-2026-113425 is a use-after-free in the mail proxy; Xint reports it with auth_http, triggered during login without valid credentials.

Code execution is Xint's claim: it reports remote code execution with worker privileges for each flaw in its tests. Some of its exploits needed more than reaching nginx. For CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-121810, nginx had to be able to open a TCP connection to the attacker, and for CVE-2026-123634, nginx's resolver had to reach the attacker's DNS server.

The sources differ on scope and severity. F5 and nginx.org list the resolver flaw from 0.6.18 and the mail proxy flaw from 0.5.33, while Xint gives 1.13.4 and 0.5.15 as the first releases for the paths it tested. nginx.org rates CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-113425 major and the other three medium. F5 also credits other researchers for CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633.

The same releases fix five further nginx vulnerabilities. The most serious, CVE-2026-118899, is an infinite loop while reading a request body over TLS 1.3 that lets an unauthenticated attacker stall a worker process, in nginx 1.13.0 and later. nginx.org rates it major and F5 rates it High (CVSS 3.1 score 7.5). nginx.org rates the other four medium or minor; most affect the stream modules, and one, CVE-2026-120993, is fixed only in 1.31.9.

Xint also reports a use-after-free in the Linux kernel's SCTP send path, present since v4.15, which it chained with CVE-2026-123007 to gain root on the host, including from nginx in a Docker container. It is withholding the details until a kernel fix is available.

As of November 18, none of the five is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Xint omitted the final exploitation steps, and the sources reviewed do not report exploitation in the wild.

Risk

Any nginx reachable directly from the Internet is at risk. Xint reports running commands as the nginx worker on HTTP/2 servers; F5 says that requires bypassing ASLR.

Affected deployments

NGINX Open Source before 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, and NGINX Plus 37.x before 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1 (37.0.7.1 or 37.2.0.1 for CVE-2026-123633), that use HTTP/2, HTTP/3, proxy_pass with variables together with SSI or mirror, or the mail proxy. F5 lists NGINX Plus R33 and later R releases as affected, with no fixed build.

Distribution packages and container images can carry backported fixes without changing the version nginx -v reports, so check the full package version against your distribution's advisory.

Recommended actions

Update nginx to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, or your vendor's fixed build, and restart it. Until then, keep nginx reachable only through Cloudflare's proxy and disable affected features you don't need.

1. Find every nginx instance, including NGINX Plus, distribution packages and container images. Run nginx -V and nginx -T on each, and note which use HTTP/2, HTTP/3 or QUIC listeners, proxy_pass with variables plus SSI or mirror, or a mail block with proxy on. If a CDN or reverse proxy sits in front, test HTTP/2 against the nginx server directly.
   - Xint exposure checks: https://xint.io/blog/nginx2root-remote-code-execution
2. Update NGINX Open Source to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, NGINX Plus to 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1, or your distribution's patched package. Then restart nginx or complete a binary upgrade, because a configuration reload does not replace the running executable.
   - F5 advisory index: https://my.f5.com/manage/s/article/K000164058
   - nginx security advisories: https://nginx.org/en/security_advisories.html
3. If you can't update yet, disable the features you don't need. For CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, set http2 off on nginx 1.25.1 and later, or remove http2 from listen directives on older versions. For CVE-2026-121810, remove QUIC listeners and set http3 off. For CVE-2026-123634, point proxy_pass at fixed upstream groups; setting mirror_request_body on is not a fix. For CVE-2026-113425, limit mail proxy listeners to trusted networks. Restart nginx so existing connections close. On hosts that don't use SCTP, install sctp /bin/false in /etc/modprobe.d/ blocks the kernel module from loading, but doesn't unload a loaded module or disable one built into the kernel.
   - Xint mitigations: https://xint.io/blog/nginx2root-remote-code-execution
   - F5 resolver advisory: https://my.f5.com/manage/s/article/K000163925
   - F5 mail proxy advisory: https://my.f5.com/manage/s/article/K000163931
4. Verify that each running nginx reports a fixed version, or that its package includes your distribution's fix. Where you disabled HTTP/2, check that openssl s_client -alpn h2 no longer negotiates h2.
   - nginx security advisories: https://nginx.org/en/security_advisories.html
5. Check for signs of exploitation: programs started by an nginx worker, for example with an auditd execve rule on the worker UID, repeated worker crashes such as signal 11, and long-lived HTTP/2 connections whose received bytes grow while logged requests stay small. Investigate any program started by a worker immediately.
   - Xint investigation guidance: https://xint.io/blog/nginx2root-remote-code-execution

Use this prompt with an agent that can inspect your infrastructure.

briefings.title: Java4Shell: remote code execution in OpenJDK
briefings.summary: Prioritize patching. Oracle released patched Java SE builds in its November update, and Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938). Update every Java runtime to Oracle's November 17 build or your vendor's fixed release, starting with Internet-facing services. Then verify the updated version is running.
briefings.contentText:
Prioritize patching · Last reviewed Nov 17, 2026

A reported out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK, tracked as Java4Shell, could let an unauthenticated attacker run code in Java applications.

Updates

- Nov 17, 2026: Oracle released patched Java SE builds (https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/cspunov2026.html) in its November update, and Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938).
- Nov 18, 2026: Cloudflare releases detections for Java4Shell as part of WAF Managed Ruleset.

Details

Calif discovered and reported CVE-2026-114938, which it calls Java4Shell. Datadog Security Labs describes it as an out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK, a flaw in the Java runtime itself rather than in a third-party library. According to Datadog, the bug is reached before an application can reject the input, so the application's own validation does not protect it.

Early reports name OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later as affected and rate the flaw 9.2 under CVSS 4.0. Oracle scores Java flaws under CVSS 3.1, and its highest Java SE score in the November update is 8.1; Aikido notes that the two figures may describe different issues.

As of November 17, the vulnerable component and the conditions for exploitation are not public, and the CVE record has not been published. Calif has said it will publish technical details after Oracle's patch release.

Risk

An unauthenticated attacker may be able to run code in a Java application before it can reject the input. Aikido had seen no reports of exploitation as of November 17.

Affected deployments

Oracle lists Java SE 8u511, 11.0.33, 17.0.21, 21.0.13, 25.0.5 and 27.0.1, GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21 and 21.0.13, and GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20.0.3 as affected by its November update. OpenJDK builds from other vendors, distribution packages, and JDKs bundled in applications or container images can be affected too.

Recommended actions

Update every Java runtime to Oracle's November 17 build or your vendor's fixed release, starting with Internet-facing services. Then verify the updated version is running.

1. Find every Java runtime you run, including JDKs bundled in applications, distribution packages such as openjdk-17, and container base images. Run java -version for each one, and check the version the running JVM reports, not only the installed package.
   - Aikido: Java builds to check: https://www.aikido.dev/blog/java-17-rce-vulnerability-cve-2026-114938
2. Update Oracle Java SE to the patched build for each line: 8u513, 11.0.33.1, 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 or 27.0.1.1.
   - Oracle Critical Security Patch Update, November 2026: https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/cspunov2026.html
   - Java SE 17.0.21.1 release notes: https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/17-0-21-1-relnotes.html
3. For Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Azul Zulu, Microsoft, Red Hat or distribution builds, install that vendor's fixed release when it is available. Its build number may differ from Oracle's.
4. Restart each updated service, because upgrading the package does not replace a JVM that is already running. Then check that each process reports the patched build, for example with jcmd <pid> VM.version.

Check Oracle's November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update (https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/cspunov2026.html), the CVE record (https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-114938) and each OpenJDK vendor's advisory for affected and fixed builds. Cite sources and retrieval dates, and note whether the CVE record is published.

2. Inventory accessible hosts, container images and applications that run Java, including JDKs bundled in applications. For each, record the Java vendor, the full version string of the running JVM (java -version, or jcmd <pid> VM.version for a running process), the installed package version, and whether the process started after the package was installed.

3. Note whether each Java service is reachable from the Internet.

Separate an installed fix from a running fix. List systems you could not assess and the access needed.

Find more information and resources at https://radar.cloudflare.com/zero-wire/java4shell

Cloudflare coverage

Service status

The vulnerability can only be triggered in specific hardware configurations, namely a x86-64 processor that supports AVX-512 VBMI, so a system is exposed only when both are true. Our investigation found that the majority of Cloudflare Java workloads are not scheduled on vulnerable systems; we took immediate action to protect the remainder.

About an hour after the patches were published, we began rolling out a JVM startup option that turns off the accelerated Base64 routine containing the bug on all Java workloads, so decoding falls back to the standard implementation.

No signs of exploits were detected. Monitoring.

Product coverage

briefings.summary: Prioritize patching. briefings.contentText:
Prioritize patching · Last reviewed Nov 11, 2026

A flaw in how React Server Components serialize several typed arrays in one payload can let an unauthenticated attacker run code on the server.

Updates

- Nov 10, 2026: The React advisory was assigned CVE-2026-126187 and added to the GitHub Advisory Database, so npm audit and Dependabot now flag affected react-server-dom packages.
- Oct 22, 2026: GitHub added the Next.js advisory to its Advisory Database, so npm audit now flags affected next versions.
- Oct 17, 2026: Hash Security published an analysis and a lab proof of concept.
- Oct 14, 2026: React and Next.js published advisories and fixed releases.

Details

React Server Components send data between server and client in a format called Flight.

According to Hash Security's analysis, the trigger is several large typed arrays that share one underlying buffer. The writer then frames the stream incorrectly, and the reader can treat attacker-controlled bytes as protocol rows that call a Server Action with arguments the attacker chooses. Command execution needs a Server Action that does something dangerous with those arguments. React's fix changes how such typed arrays are written.

In Next.js, the path is an App Router app with Cache Components and a use cache function that returns several typed arrays. Versions 16.0.0 to 16.4.0 are affected. Next.js 15 is not listed in the advisory, but 15.5.28 includes React's transport protocol fix and a separate critical image optimization fix (CVE-2026-96889).

React describes the affected cases as extremely rare, and Vercel says there is no workaround.

On November 10, the React advisory was assigned CVE-2026-126187 and added to the GitHub Advisory Database, so npm audit and Dependabot now flag affected react-server-dom packages. The Next.js advisory has no CVE ID.

Risk

An unauthenticated attacker can run code in rare apps whose RSC payloads mix several typed arrays with attacker input. Public proof-of-concept code exists; React, Vercel and CISA had not reported exploitation as of November 11.

Affected deployments

Next.js 16.0.0–16.4.0 apps that use the App Router with Cache Components. Also other RSC frameworks or bundler setups with react-server-dom-webpack, -turbopack or -parcel 19.x before 19.0.9, 19.1.10, 19.2.9 or 19.3.1. Next.js 15.5 is not listed in the advisory, but 15.5.28 includes React's transport fix, so update 15.5 apps too. Apps that don't render React on a server are not affected.

Recommended actions

Update Next.js to 16.4.1 or later (15.5.28 on 15.x) or react-server-dom-* to a fixed 19.x release, then check the deployed version. Updating React alone does not fix Next.js.

1. Find apps that use React Server Components. Check lockfiles for next and the react-server-dom-* packages, including monorepo workspaces and container images.
2. Update Next.js 16 apps to 16.4.1 or later, and Next.js 15.5 apps to 15.5.28 or later. Next.js ships its own compiled copy of the RSC packages, so the fix only arrives through the next package.
   - Next.js advisory: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/security/advisories/GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr
   - Next.js security update: https://nextjs.org/blog/nextjs-security-update-october-14-2026
3. For other RSC frameworks or custom bundler setups, update react-server-dom-* to 19.0.9, 19.1.10, 19.2.9 or 19.3.1, or to the framework release that includes them.
   - React advisory: https://github.com/react/react/security/advisories/GHSA-xqc2-xf4c-x3h3
4. Rebuild and redeploy, then check the version in the deployed image or artifact, for example node_modules/next/package.json. A fixed lockfile alone does not show that the fix is running.

Perform a read-only assessment within your authorized access. Do not send crafted payloads, run proof-of-concept code, change dependencies or redeploy.

1. Verify the React advisory at https://github.com/react/react/security/advisories/GHSA-xqc2-xf4c-x3h3 and the Next.js advisory at https://github.com/vercel/next.js/security/advisories/GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr. Establish affected and fixed versions. Cite sources and retrieval dates.

2. Inventory accessible repositories, monorepo workspaces and container images. From lockfiles (package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, yarn.lock, bun.lock), record the resolved versions of next, react-server-dom-webpack, react-server-dom-turbopack and react-server-dom-parcel. 3. Vercel advises upgrading regardless, so treat this as prioritization, not a reason to skip the update.

4. Where deployment metadata is available, check that the running build matches the lockfile you assessed.

briefings.title: *sshole: OpenSSH password bypass on musl Linux
briefings.summary: Prioritize patching. OpenSSH released 10.6p2, Alpine published fixed packages back to 3.16, and CVE-2026-123158 was assigned. briefings.contentText:
Prioritize patching · Last reviewed Nov 6, 2026

An authentication bypass in OpenSSH's sshd on musl-based Linux without PAM, including Alpine's default package, lets attackers log in to accounts with no password set.

Updates

- Nov 5, 2026: OpenSSH released 10.6p2, Alpine published fixed packages back to 3.16, and CVE-2026-123158 was assigned.

Details

When sshd is built without PAM, it checks a password by hashing the attempt with the C library's crypt() and comparing the result to the account's stored password field. Accounts with no password set store * in that field, which normally matches nothing.

musl's crypt() returns the string * as an error value when the password is longer than 256 bytes. sshd compares that * to the stored *, finds a match and accepts the login. The attack needs one other account on the machine with a $5$ or $6$ password hash, because sshd borrows its salt. One such account makes every account without a password reachable.

The flaw dates to 2016 and was reported by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield. OpenSSH 10.6p2 adds a workaround in sshd; OpenSSH considers the root cause to be outside sshd. Alpine backported the fix to every branch from 3.16, so a lower OpenSSH version number does not mean a host is still vulnerable.

Alpine's official tiny-cloud images from 3.18.11 through 3.24.3 ship an alpine user with no password and passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot but become exploitable once any $6$ hash exists on the machine, for example after an admin sets a console password. An attacker can then log in as alpine and use doas to become root, even though root itself is reachable only if PermitRootLogin yes is set.

Not affected: glibc systems, Alpine's openssh-server-pam package with UsePAM yes, and accounts locked with !. According to Alpine, cloud images configured through cloud-init are not affected either, because cloud-init writes PasswordAuthentication no unless user-data sets ssh_pwauth: true.

Risk

With password logins enabled, an unauthenticated attacker can log in to passwordless accounts if another account has a $5$ or $6$ hash. Neither OpenSSH nor Alpine had reported exploitation as of November 6.

Affected deployments

Hosts running OpenSSH sshd before 10.6p2 and without their distribution's backported fix, on musl-based Linux such as Alpine (the researcher also lists OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto builds running OpenSSH) without PAM and with PasswordAuthentication enabled. Targets are accounts whose password field is * and directory-service users via musl-nscd, which have no shadow entry.

Recommended actions

Update OpenSSH to 10.6p2 or your distribution's fixed package, then restart sshd. If you cannot update yet, set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd.

1. Find hosts running sshd on musl-based Linux, including Alpine VMs, cloud images, appliances and containers that run sshd. Check whether sshd uses PAM and whether PasswordAuthentication is enabled, including inside Match blocks in sshd_config and its drop-in files.
2. Update OpenSSH to 10.6p2 or your distribution's fixed package. On Alpine, run apk upgrade -U -a, then compare the version shown by apk list -I 'openssh*' with the advisory's fixed version for your branch. Alpine's fixed packages keep older version numbers, so sshd -V alone does not show the fix.
   - Alpine Linux advisory: https://alpinelinux.org/posts/2026-11-05-openssh-password-authentication-bypass/
   - OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes: https://www.openssh.org/releasenotes.html#10.6p2
3. Restart sshd (rc-service sshd restart on Alpine). Upgrading the package does not replace the running daemon.
4. If you cannot update yet, set PasswordAuthentication no, including in any Match block that enables it. Check the configuration with sshd -t, restart sshd and confirm that sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication shows PasswordAuthentication set to no; for Match blocks, test with sshd -T -C user=…,host=…,addr=…. Keep an existing key-based session open while you test.
5. Check /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account with no password, such as alpine, root, a key-only user or a directory-service user. If you find one or cannot rule out a login, treat the host as compromised and review doas use, new users, changed files and authorized_keys.

Use this prompt with an agent that can inspect your infrastructure.

Assess whether the infrastructure available to you is affected by CVE-2026-123158 (*sshole), the OpenSSH password authentication bypass on musl-based Linux without PAM. Perform a read-only assessment within your authorized access. Do not attempt logins with long passwords, change sshd configuration or restart services.

1. Verify the current CVE record at https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-123158, the OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes at https://www.openssh.org/releasenotes.html#10.6p2 and the Alpine advisory at https://alpinelinux.org/posts/2026-11-05-openssh-password-authentication-bypass/. Establish affected and fixed versions, including Alpine's backported package versions. Cite sources and retrieval dates.

2. Inventory accessible hosts, VMs, cloud images, appliances and containers that run sshd. For each, record the C library (musl or glibc), the installed openssh package and version, whether the running sshd started after the package was installed, whether it uses PAM (openssh-server vs openssh-server-pam and UsePAM), and the effective PasswordAuthentication value from sshd -T. sshd -T without -C ignores Match blocks, so also inspect Match blocks in sshd_config and its drop-ins, or test them with sshd -T -C. Get the installed package release with apk list -I 'openssh*' on Alpine and compare it with the advisory's fixed version, not the version sshd -V prints.

3. Where you have access, list accounts whose /etc/shadow password field is exactly * and whether any account has a $5$ or $6$ hash. Do not print hashes; record only the field type. Note directory-service users without shadow entries, and accounts with passwordless doas or sudo.

4. Search /var/log/messages or the journal for sshd 'Accepted password for' entries on accounts with no password, and note any found.

Return a concise summary and a table: host | libc | openssh package/version | sshd restarted after update | PAM | PasswordAuthentication | * and $5$/$6$ accounts present | assessment (affected, fixed, not applicable or unknown) | evidence | next action. Separate an installed fix from a running fix, and patch status from evidence of compromise. List hosts you could not assess and the access needed.

Find more information and resources at https://radar.cloudflare.com/zero-wire/sshole

Cloudflare coverage

Service status

No impact to Cloudflare infrastructure.

Product coverage

This attack targets SSH, not HTTP, so WAF rules do not apply.

Evidence and sources

CVE record
Rated High, CVSS 3.1 8.1. CISA's assessment lists a public proof of concept and does not consider the attack automatable.
- CVE-2026-123158: https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-123158

Vendor advisories
Alpine lists the conditions for exposure, fixed package versions per branch, cloud image impact and how to check for compromise.
- OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes: https://www.openssh.org/releasenotes.html#10.6p2
- Alpine Linux advisory: https://alpinelinux.org/posts/2026-11-05-openssh-password-authentication-bypass/
- OpenSSH fix commit: https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/commit/4353fdc43ef646c43a8dda7025cc1a898caf1482

cloud-init configuration
cloud-init's default config sets ssh_pwauth: false for Alpine, so it writes PasswordAuthentication no unless user-data sets ssh_pwauth: true.
- cloud-init 26.2 default config (Alpine): https://github.com/canonical/cloud-init/blob/26.2/config/cloud.cfg.tmpl#L63-L76
- cloud-init ssh_pwauth reference: https://docs.cloud-init.io/en/latest/reference/modules.html#mod-cc-set-passwords

Original research
The researcher's check script compares sshd's version number, so it can report Alpine's backported fixed packages as exposed.
- *sshole disclosure: https://sshhole.com/
- Exposure check script and proof of concept: https://github.com/oz9un/sshole

Disclosure announcement
- oss-security post: https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/11/05/3

briefings.contentText:
Prioritize patching · Last reviewed Nov 9, 2026

PHP runtime flaws can let unauthenticated attackers run code; a related session upload progress flaw affects applications with specific session settings.

Updates

- Nov 3, 2026: Cloudflare updated detection for php2shell WAF rules #2 and #3 (https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/change-log/changelog/#2026-11-03) in the Free and Managed Rulesets, based on PHP CTF reports.
- Oct 30, 2026: Cloudflare updated detection for php2shell WAF rules #3 and #4 (https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/change-log/changelog/#2026-10-30:~:text=WAF%20Release%20%2D%202026%2D10%2D30,-This%20release%20introduces) in the Free and Managed Rulesets, and reported that PHP CTF submissions helped harden protections and create new detections.
- Oct 28, 2026: Cloudflare updated detection for php2shell WAF rule #6 (https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/change-log/changelog/#2026-10-28) in the Free and Managed Rulesets, based on PHP CTF reports.
- Oct 27, 2026: Cloudflare launched its PHP Capture the Flag challenge to test WAF protections through the Bug Bounty program.
- Oct 26, 2026: CISA added the original CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 vulnerabilities to KEV.
- Oct 23, 2026: PHP published its session upload progress informational advisory for the related CVE-2026-115560, describing unusual serializer configuration prerequisites and recommending disabling upload progress pending the next regular bugfix release.
- Oct 23, 2026: Cloudflare confirmed that php2shell WAF rule #6 (https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/change-log/changelog/#2026-10-23) in the Free and Managed Rulesets also covers CVE-2026-115560.
- Oct 21, 2026: Cloudflare added seven php2shell WAF rules (https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/change-log/changelog/#2026-10-21) to the Free and Managed Rulesets, with Block as the default action, and published mitigation guidance.
- Oct 21, 2026: PHP published its initial security guidance for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

Details

php2shell is the name used for two PHP runtime vulnerabilities disclosed on 21 October: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. They affect how PHP manages memory when processing an HTTP request fails unexpectedly, including when memory is exhausted.

Normally PHP allocates memory to process a request and safely releases it when work finishes. In these cases, an error can interrupt that process. PHP may then use internal data that was never fully initialized, or later follow references to memory that has already been released.

An attacker can send specially crafted HTTP traffic to trigger those conditions. The result can range from a crashed PHP process to information disclosure or attacker-controlled code execution. Updating website code or a plugin alone does not fix the runtime defect.

Related follow-up: CVE-2026-115560. PHP's 23 October informational advisory describes an additional RCE vector involving session upload progress. It requires upload progress to remain enabled and the application to switch its session serializer from php_binary or php_serialize to php at runtime, using ini_set() before session_start(). The advisory recommends disabling session upload progress pending the next regular bugfix release; applications that never change the serializer at runtime can keep the feature enabled. Patching the original php2shell vulnerabilities does not establish that this follow-up is addressed.

Risk

CISA lists the original two flaws as known exploited. The separate session upload progress flaw was not in CISA's catalog on November 9.

Affected deployments

Review PHP 5.4 or later serving web requests: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix the original two flaws, and older branches need a vendor backport. The follow-up affects applications that enable session upload progress and change the serializer at runtime before starting a session.

Recommended actions

Update the PHP runtime using the vendor advisory, and assess CVE-2026-115560 separately. Ask your hosting provider to confirm fixes if it manages PHP.

1. Identify Internet-facing applications running PHP and establish their runtime version.
2. Update PHP to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or install your vendor's backported fix, including through managed hosting providers.
   - PHP security advisory: https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-21-5
3. Review the session upload progress advisory for CVE-2026-115560 separately, including application serializer changes and any vendor updates that supersede its interim guidance.
   - PHP session upload progress advisory: https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-23-1
4. Review logs and incident-response processes for suspicious PHP request activity.
5. Keep edge mitigations enabled while the update is being deployed.

Use this prompt with an agent that can inspect your infrastructure.

Assess whether the infrastructure available to you is affected by the original php2shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) and the related session upload progress issue CVE-2026-115560. Perform a read-only assessment within your authorized access. Do not send exploit payloads, trigger memory exhaustion, or change systems.

1. Verify the current PHP advisories at https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-21-5 and https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-23-1, along with any superseding PHP, operating-system, or hosting-provider advisories. Establish affected and fixed releases or interim guidance for each CVE, including vendor backports. Cite sources and retrieval dates; flag anything you cannot verify. Report applicability, patch status, and exploitation evidence separately for each of the three CVEs. Do not extend CISA KEV evidence for the original two vulnerabilities to CVE-2026-115560.

2. Inventory PHP across accessible hosts, containers, Kubernetes workloads, images, and managed hosting, including WordPress, Magento, and other PHP applications. Record the service, environment, owner where known, runtime/package version, and image digest or build identity. Distinguish running deployments from repository declarations and unused images. Check the PHP runtime actually serving requests (for example PHP-FPM or Apache), not just the CLI version. If updates were installed, verify that running processes and replicas use the updated build.

3. Compare each deployed runtime against authoritative advisories for the original two CVEs. Do not treat an older version string as vulnerable if the vendor documents a backported fix, or an updated application/plugin as evidence that PHP itself is patched. Identify Internet-facing and internal request paths, including origins reachable directly. Record access gaps; absence of PHP in one repository does not establish its absence across the infrastructure.

4. Assess CVE-2026-115560 separately. Inspect effective session.upload_progress.enabled and session.serialize_handler configuration, and application code that uses ini_set() to switch the serializer from php_binary or php_serialize to php before session_start(). Verify the relevant request-handling configuration rather than relying on CLI defaults. If configuration or code is inaccessible, report unknown. Follow current vendor guidance to distinguish fixed, mitigated, and not-applicable deployments; do not assume that updates for the original two CVEs also resolve this follow-up. Report findings without changing settings.

5. Report WAF or other compensating controls separately from runtime patch status. Where configuration is accessible, check whether relevant traffic is proxied, applicable rules are enabled in Block, and exceptions or bypass paths exist. Verify coverage for each CVE rather than assuming one php2shell rule covers every path. A WAF rule, blocked attack, or lack of alerts does not prove that the runtime is patched or that compromise has not occurred.

Return a concise summary and a table: asset/service | deployed runtime/build | assessment per CVE (affected, fixed, not applicable, or unknown) | compensating controls | exposure | supporting evidence | next action. Prioritize affected Internet-facing services. List unassessed systems and the exact evidence or access needed to resolve unknowns. Link to current vendor remediation guidance and propose verification steps without applying changes. Do not conclude that the entire infrastructure is unaffected unless the assessed scope supports that conclusion.

Find more information and resources at https://radar.cloudflare.com/zero-wire/php2shell

Cloudflare coverage

Service status

No impact to Cloudflare identified; monitoring

We have found no impact to Cloudflare from PHP2Shell. When the vulnerabilities were disclosed, our security and engineering teams rolled out mitigations and patches across Cloudflare's PHP systems to prevent impact. We also tested our security posture against these vulnerabilities. Our review continues, and we will update this notice if anything changes.

Product coverage

The Cloudflare Free and Managed Rulesets each include seven PHP Remote Code Execution Attack rules for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, with Block as the default action; rule #6 in each also covers CVE-2026-115560. The rules are a compensating control, not a fix for the vulnerable PHP runtime.

- PHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, CVE-2026-115560) #6: Default action: Block · Free plans, Paid plans
- PHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) #7: Default action: Block · Free plans, Paid plans

- Paid plans: https://dash.cloudflare.com/?to=%2F%3Aaccount%2F%3Azone%2Fsecurity%2Fsecurity-rules%2Fmanaged-rules%2Fruleset%2Fefb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee%2Frules&search=CVE-2026-109618

Perform a read-only assessment within your authorized access. Do not send exploit payloads, trigger memory exhaustion, or change systems.

Verify the current PHP advisories at https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-21-5 and https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-23-1, along with any superseding PHP, operating-system, or hosting-provider advisories. briefings.contentText:
Prioritize patching · Last reviewed Nov 2, 2026

A race condition in Linux's IPv4 TCP connection handling can expose kernel memory, crash a host, or allow remote code execution before application authentication.

Updates

- Nov 1, 2026: Atlas updated its distribution review to report fixed RHEL kernels and remaining vendor-specific patch gaps.
- Oct 30, 2026: Red Hat published a Critical-impact bulletin and interim network-filtering guidance.
- Oct 29, 2026: The Go Security Team published MPTCP applicability guidance, subsequently mirrored on oss-security.
- Oct 27, 2026: Anthropic disclosed a working research exploit for remote root command execution against MPTCP listeners.
- Oct 15, 2026: The Linux kernel CNA published the CVE record with upstream fix references.

Details

CVE-2026-98432 is a use-after-free in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP handshake. One operation can free stored IPv4 options while another CPU is still reading them to construct a connection reply. The flaw dates to Linux 4.4. The Linux kernel CNA rates it Critical, with a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8.

The vulnerable processing happens before an application authenticates a connection. A remote peer can trigger a race that discloses kernel memory, corrupts memory, or crashes the host. Anthropic demonstrated root command execution on servers exposing a Multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener.

The Go Security Team warns that the underlying bug is not specific to MPTCP and that similar attacks may be possible without MPTCP listeners. Its guidance notes that Go programs enable MPTCP listeners by default on Linux from Go 1.24, subject to configuration. Disabling MPTCP is not a substitute for patching the kernel.

The upstream fix defers freeing the options until concurrent readers have finished. Distribution vendors backport the fix under their own package versions. Updating an application or rebuilding a container image alone does not patch the host kernel, and installing a new kernel does not by itself prove that the running kernel is fixed.

Risk

Researchers demonstrated root command execution against MPTCP listeners; other IPv4 TCP services may also be affected. Reports reviewed on November 2 did not confirm real-world attacks.

Affected deployments

Linux hosts with an affected kernel and IPv4 TCP networking, including container hosts and Kubernetes nodes. Prioritize reachable MPTCP listeners; other IPv4 TCP services may also be affected.

Recommended actions

Install your distribution's fixed kernel and verify it is running after a reboot or vendor-supported activation. Updating containers alone does not patch the host.

1. Inventory running Linux kernels and reachable IPv4 TCP services, including container hosts, Kubernetes nodes, appliances, and managed infrastructure.
2. Check the running kernel against your distribution or platform advisory, including any backported fixes.
   - Red Hat kernel advisory: https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026-016
   - Linux CVE record: https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-98432
3. Install the fixed kernel, prioritizing Internet-facing hosts and MPTCP listeners. Reboot or use the vendor-supported activation procedure, then verify that the running kernel includes the fix.
4. Where a patch cannot yet be applied, consult vendor mitigation guidance. Red Hat describes IPv4-option filtering as exposure reduction, not complete prevention; verify compatibility with your network and workloads.

Use this prompt with an agent that can inspect your infrastructure.

Assess whether the infrastructure available to you is affected by CVE-2026-98432, the Linux IPv4 TCP use-after-free vulnerability. Perform a read-only assessment within your authorized access. Do not send exploit packets, stress-test listeners, change firewall rules, or reboot systems.

1. Verify the current Linux CVE record at https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-98432 and the relevant distribution or platform vendor advisories. Consult https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026-016 and the Go Security Team's applicability guidance at https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/10/30/1 where relevant. Establish affected and fixed builds, including vendor backports. Cite sources and retrieval dates; flag anything you cannot verify.

2. Inventory accessible Linux hosts, virtual machines, container hosts, Kubernetes nodes, appliances, and managed platforms. Record the asset, environment, owner where known, distribution, running kernel release/build, installed kernel packages, and any verified livepatch status. Use read-only evidence such as uname -r, uname -v, package metadata, and platform inventory. Match vendor fixes to the running kernel, not merely an installed update or an image tag. Containers share their host's kernel: rebuilding an application image does not patch it. If host access is unavailable, record that gap and request confirmation from the operator or provider.

3. Identify Internet-facing and internal IPv4 TCP listeners and the paths that can reach them, including direct-origin access, load balancers, and container networks. Check MPTCP listeners and configuration in relevant network namespaces using read-only inspection such as ss -Mlnp and sysctl net.mptcp.enabled where supported. Review Go services and their MPTCP settings. An enabled sysctl alone does not prove that an MPTCP listener exists; an empty result without sufficient access does not establish absence across the host. Prioritize exposed MPTCP listeners, but do not classify a kernel as unaffected simply because MPTCP is disabled or no such listener was found.

4. Assess network-layer compensating controls separately from kernel patch status. Where accessible, inspect filtering of IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options and whether alternate or container-network paths bypass it. Do not confuse IPv4 options with TCP options or claim that filtering fully fixes the vulnerability. HTTP WAF rules do not address this pre-HTTP TCP-handshake flaw. A proxy or firewall configuration alone does not establish that every path to the host is protected.

Return a concise summary and a table: asset/host | running kernel/build | assessment (affected, fixed, not applicable, or unknown) | IPv4/MPTCP exposure | supporting evidence | next action. Separate kernel applicability from network reachability. Prioritize affected Internet-facing systems, identify installed-but-not-active fixes, and link to current vendor remediation and activation guidance. List unassessed systems and the exact evidence or access needed to resolve unknowns. Distinguish a demonstrated research exploit from exploitation in the wild; do not infer absence of compromise from patch status or a lack of alerts. Propose verification steps without applying changes, and limit conclusions to the scope actually assessed.

Find more information and resources at https://radar.cloudflare.com/zero-wire/linux-ipv4-tcp-use-after-free

Cloudflare coverage

Service status

Cloudflare was not impacted by this vulnerability.

Product coverage

Magic Transit customers can use Cloudflare Network Firewall to reduce exposure by filtering IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options before they reach their infrastructure. Coverage depends on routing and firewall configuration and does not replace kernel patching.

Evidence and sources

CVE record
The Linux kernel CNA documents the race condition, upstream affected and fixed branches, and Critical CVSS 3.1 severity of 9.8. Distribution package versions must be checked against vendor advisories.
- CVE-2026-98432: https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-98432

Vendor advisory
Red Hat describes unauthenticated remote code execution potential and broad IPv4 TCP exposure. Its interim filtering guidance reduces exposure but does not replace kernel updates.
- Red Hat RHSB-2026-016: https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026-016

Runtime applicability
The Go Security Team explains MPTCP listener defaults and warns that systems without MPTCP listeners may still be vulnerable to similar attacks.
- Go Security Team advisory: https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/10/30/1

Exploit evidence
Anthropic demonstrates root command execution on Linux servers with MPTCP listeners.
- Anthropic research disclosure: https://www.anthropic.com/research/discovering-vulnerabilities-with-claude

CISA KEV
CVE-2026-98432 was not present in the CISA KEV feed retrieved on 2 November 2026 (catalog version 2026.10.30). Absence from KEV is not evidence that exploitation cannot occur.
- CISA KEV catalog: https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog

Product coverage
Magic Transit includes Cloudflare Network Firewall. Its IPv4 header-length field supports filtering packets carrying IP options; this is a configurable exposure-reduction capability, not a verified default-on CVE-specific mitigation.
- Magic Transit network filtering: https://developers.cloudflare.com/magic-transit/ddos/
- Cloudflare Network Firewall fields: https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-network-firewall/reference/network-firewall-fields/

Technical analysis and distribution tracking
Atlas provides a technical explanation and links to distribution patch trackers. Its 1 November update reports RHEL fixes and outstanding updates elsewhere; consult each vendor for current availability.
- Atlas Linux IPv4 TCP analysis: https://atlasum.net/blog/cve-2026-98432-linux-ipv4-tcp-uaf

briefings.contentText:
Review trust settings · Last reviewed Nov 2, 2026

Eight compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates could enable server impersonation and interception of traffic where affected certificates remain trusted.

Updates

- Oct 30, 2026: Cloudflare published follow-up research on forged certificates, client patching progress, and the limitations of its measurements.
- Oct 21, 2026: Cloudflare updated its response and customer action table.
- Oct 20, 2026: Cloudflare published the certificate-compromise response and recommended customer actions.

Details

A compromise of intermediate certificate authorities can allow an attacker holding a fraudulent but trusted certificate to impersonate a service or intercept traffic. The risk depends on whether a client or service still trusts the affected intermediates.

This is a certificate-trust incident, not a CVE-scored software vulnerability. It requires a different response: review trust stores and client software as well as applications and infrastructure that perform certificate validation.

Cloudflare's follow-up reports certificates forged using the weak keys and continued acceptance of affected chains among sampled clients. Forged certificates alone do not establish successful interception. The client measurements come from challenge-page traffic with a skewed, bot-heavy sample; they are not an Internet-wide patch-rate estimate.

Risk

Researchers found that some clients still accepted affected certificate chains, allowing forged certificates to pass validation.

Affected deployments

Clients and services that still trust the affected eMudhra intermediates. Check customer-managed trust stores, origins and mutual TLS configurations.

Recommended actions

Apply the trust-store and client updates in the official response to systems that still trust the affected intermediates.

1. Identify customer-managed clients, origins, mutual TLS configurations, and container images that may trust the affected intermediates.
2. Apply the product-specific client and trust-store updates in the official response.
   - Cloudflare certificate-compromise response: https://blog.cloudflare.com/emudhra-certificate-compromise/
3. Review certificate-validation and outbound HTTPS paths that are not managed by Cloudflare.

Cloudflare coverage

Service status

As reported on 30 October, all high-priority Cloudflare systems were patched; lower-impact remediation remained in progress.

Product coverage

No WAF rules are applicable to this certificate-trust incident.

Affected certificates and the actions required for each Cloudflare product.

Assess your exposure · Last reviewed Oct 25, 2026

CVE-2026-111497 is a memory-corruption flaw in the shared Brotli decoder. Any service that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli, in a request or an HTTP response, can be exposed.

Updates

- Oct 25, 2026: Cloudflare documented two WAF rules and their default Log action.
- Oct 21, 2026: Node.js published security-release guidance for the vulnerability.

Details

node2shell is the early name for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder. The decoder can mistake a malformed block switch for a temporary lack of input, continue appending bytes to a small internal buffer, and corrupt process memory.

The name can be misleading: the flaw is in a widely reused Brotli library, not in Node.js alone. It can reach applications through runtimes, HTTP clients, framework middleware, and container images that bundle or install the decoder.

In Node.js, applications can reach the decoder through node:zlib or Brotli-aware request middleware. Node.js built-in fetch is powered by Undici and automatically handles Brotli responses, so server-side URL fetches and remote-image features require review too. Next.js remote image optimization is one such path. Gzip, Deflate, and Zstd use different decoders. Remediation guidance was still developing at the October 25 review.

Risk

The decoder is used beyond Node.js, including in server-side fetches. The October 25 review did not confirm active exploitation.

Affected deployments

Services that use a vulnerable Brotli decoder, including bundled copies in runtimes and container images. Node.js request middleware and server-side fetches both need review.

Recommended actions

Update or remove vulnerable Brotli decoders using each vendor's guidance, including copies bundled with runtimes or container images.

1. Inventory runtimes, HTTP libraries, dependencies, and container images that provide Brotli decoding.
2. Apply the security update or vendor guidance for every affected component, then rebuild and redeploy affected workloads.
   - Node.js security advisory: https://nodejs.org/en/blog/vulnerability/october-2026-security-releases#nodejs-brotli-decoder-out-of-bounds-write-permits-remote-code-execution-cve-2026-111497---high
3. Prioritize inbound Brotli request handling and outbound fetch, webhook, crawler, URL-preview, proxy, and remote-image features that retrieve untrusted responses.

Service status

No impact; Brotli is not currently used in Cloudflare infrastructure.

Product coverage

Cloudflare has WAF rules for documented Node2Shell request patterns. They default to Log and customers must configure them to Block if blocking mitigation is needed.

Details

briefings.summary: Update affected systems. Cloudflare updated its response with vulnerability and remediation guidance. Check each site's WordPress version and apply the vendor's update or backport guidance. Keep compensating controls in place during remediation.
briefings.contentText:
Update affected systems · Last reviewed Jul 20, 2026

Two related WordPress flaws can expose database contents and allow unauthenticated code execution through distinct SQL-injection and REST API attack paths.

Updates

- Jul 20, 2026: Cloudflare updated its response with vulnerability and remediation guidance.
- Jul 17, 2026: WordPress published the security release and Cloudflare published its WAF response.

Details

CVE-2026-60137 is a SQL-injection issue and CVE-2026-63030 is an unauthenticated code-execution issue associated with a REST API attack path. Their affected versions and conditions differ.

Managed WAF rules can mitigate known requests, but do not repair WordPress installations or replace vendor updates.

Risk

Affected sites can be compromised before sign-in. The July 20 review did not confirm active exploitation.

Affected deployments

WordPress sites running a release affected by either CVE. Check the security release for each flaw's version and configuration requirements.

Recommended actions

Check each site's WordPress version and apply the vendor's update or backport guidance. Keep compensating controls in place during remediation.

1. Identify WordPress sites and compare their versions with the WordPress security release.
   - WordPress security release: https://wordpress.org/news/2026/07/wordpress-7-0-2-release/
2. Apply the vendor update or backport guidance for each affected deployment.
3. Confirm that Internet-facing WordPress traffic follows the intended security controls during remediation.

Cloudflare coverage

Service status

No impact to Cloudflare. We do not use WordPress on our infrastructure.

Product coverage

Cloudflare has WAF rules for documented WordPress exploit paths. They are a compensating control, not a replacement for updating WordPress.
